newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African shortage reflects fwd mkt moves - Cross.
newsitem.headline: S.African shortage reflects fwd mkt moves - Cross.

text.p: The rise in South Africa's money market shortage was a reflection of the Reserve Bank's continuing withdrawal from the forward foreign exchange market, deputy governor James Cross said on Wednesday.
The central bank said earlier that the shortage jumped to 8.496 billion rand on Tuesday from 7.757 billion rand on Monday.
The shortage has now risen nearly 3.5 billion rand from the 5.092 billion rand registered on June 30 -- its lowest level this year.
The bank has previously stated its intention to slowly withdraw from the South African forward market.
"In doing that we deliver a lot of forwards to the market every month which has an effect on the shortage because we give dollars to the banks and they give us rands," Cross said.

"The higher shortage has an effect of pushing forward premiums up and the higher premiums make forward cover slightly less attractive, so the forward cover balances tend to reduce and we slowly achieve what we want to achieve," he said.
He added that during the first half of the year the central bank's net open position had declined significantly, but declined to specify by what amount.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said in April that the bank's net oversold position amounted to $21.2 billion on March 31 from $22.2 billion at the end of last year.
A senior money market trader said there was currently a mismatch in the maturities of commercial banks' books, which was likely to remain in place for the next few days.
"At the moment the way they are structured is they need to get rand in to cover their maturing books," the trader said.
"Over the next three or four days they will be needing to attract rand for their dollar maturities...the shortage should go back to normal next week," he said.
Traders said the market had shrugged off the higher shortage as a short-term hiccup, but that call rates -- currently around 15.15 percent -- could edge higher later in the day.
"At this point the market sees it as a temporary aberration and it has not spilled over as a source of concern as yet," one senior trader said.
"If it stays at these levels then the market might have to reassess the situation, but right now the market is just taking it in its stride," he added.
Short-term deposit rates were quoted steady at between 15.65 and 15.70 percent offered, while the 90-day BA rate was also unmoved at 15.10 percent.
On the forward market, rates were all quoted higher across the one- to 12-month area.
